title: Accent Change May Be Sign of a Good Ear — Study
paragraphs: If you spend time with someone who speaks with a different accent than you, you may start to sound like them. Or they may start to sound like you!
But no matter how much time you spend together, you both probably won't sound exactly the same — and researchers aren't sure why.
A new study looked at 136 people who speak English with an American accent.
They were first asked to read a list of words aloud. Next, they were told to listen to a recording of a woman saying the same words with an Australian accent.
The participants were then asked to read the words aloud again. However, they received three different types of instructions.
Some were told to read in their normal accent. Some were told to imitate the Australian speaker as closely as possible. And some received no instruction.
The results showed that people could copy the Australian accent when asked to. And when told to speak normally, most people kept their American accent.
However, those who received no instruction tended to copy just one part of the Australian accent — dropping the "r" sound in certain words.
Participants were also asked what they noticed about the woman's accent. The most common answers were the way she pronounced the letter "r," and the vowel sound in words like "bath."
The researchers found that participants who noticed these sounds tended to copy them more. This was true whether they had been asked to imitate the woman or had received no instructions.

"Basically, if we don't tell you whether or not to imitate somebody, you're going to sound like them on the bits that you notice or think are interesting," researcher Kathryn Campbell-Kibler explained.
So maybe if your accent changes more than others', it means your ears notice those differences more!
